item.title: Jio Platforms IPO anchor investor quota nearly 30 times oversubscribed
item.description: Jio Platforms is set to raise up to $3.2 billion at a valuation of $108.3 billion in what will be India's biggest ever IPO ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Mukesh Ambani's $3.2 billion Jio Platforms IPO has drawn bids from institutions including GIC, BlackRock and Fidelity, totaling almost 30 times the quota reserved for anchor investors, a person with direct knowledge said.The telecoms, cloud and AI group on Monday opened its record initial public offering to institutional investors who can bid for up to 30% of the offering reserved exclusively for them, before the issue opens for public subscription on Wednesday.Jio Platforms is set to raise up to $3.2 billion at a valuation of $108.3 billion in what will be India's biggest ever IPO.Fidelity, Singapore's GIC, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and BlackRock were among the investors to place bids for the institutional quota, the person told Reuters.Reliance, which is the ultimate owner of Jio Platforms, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.ADIA, BlackRock, Fidelity and GIC did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

item.title: Elon Musk says he will gift SpaceX shares to 'every kid in America'
item.description: Musk is by far the world’s richest person with a net worth of more than $900 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His SpaceX shares account for the vast majority of that wealth, at ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Mark Bergen Elon Musk pledged to distribute a share of SpaceX to each American child after competitor Anthropic PBC said it would set aside a portion of its shares for the public benefit.   “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” the company’s chief executive officer wrote on X, the social media platform he owns. “This will be the first of many.”  It’s not clear how such share contributions would work, and Musk did not elaborate on his donation plans.  His post came after Anthropic disclosed plans to place 5% of its shares in a fund to make donations that address “the public good.” Regulators across the globe have increased calls for regulating artificial intelligence after insiders flagged the possibility of catastrophic scenarios. Anthropic, which is preparing for a blockbuster public listing, has frequently raised concerns about broad societal risks and dangers of AI. The Claude developer said some of its new fund would go to addressing the “labor market impacts” of the technology.  After Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday, Musk replied to the company’s X account to say he recommends giving shares “directly to the public.”   Musk is by far the world’s richest person with a net worth of more than $900 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His SpaceX shares account for the vast majority of that wealth, at about $700 billion, with the rest coming from Tesla Inc., Boring Co. and Neuralink. The billionaire has a history of floating ideas that don’t materialize or suggesting plans he later explains away as jokes. Musk pinned his latest post about SpaceX shares to the top of his X page.

item.title: Albania protests: Why are people demanding Edi Rama's resignation?
item.description: Albania is witnessing days of anti-government protests and clashes as demonstrators demand Edi Rama's resignation. Here is what to know about the unrest ...
item.dc:creator: Sarjna Rai
item.content:encoded: Albania is witnessing anti-government protests, with demonstrators demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation amid corruption allegations against senior officials. The demonstrations have escalated in Tirana, the capital, with reports of clashes and a fire at the country’s Supreme Court building, raising concerns about political stability and Albania’s ambitions to join the European Union (EU). What is happening in Albania? The protests entered their sixth consecutive day on Sunday, October 18, with thousands gathering in Tirana to demand Rama’s resignation. Demonstrations have also spread to other cities, drawing more people into the protests against the government. According to Reuters, protesters targeted government buildings and banks, damaged property and threw paving stones at police. Security forces responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets, while several protesters and police officers were injured. The protests have also seen incidents of arson at government buildings in Tirana. According to Al Jazeera, a fire broke out in the Supreme Court building on Sunday, while an earlier blaze was reported at the Education Ministry. The protests have intensified pressure on Rama, who has been in power since 2013 and won a fourth consecutive term in last year’s parliamentary election. ALSO READ: France unrest: Macron urges calm after 2,400 arrests amid riots, looting Why are people protesting in Albania? The latest protests reflect growing dissatisfaction with the government over corruption allegations, economic pressures and the quality of public services. Although student demands have helped fuel the current demonstrations, the unrest follows months of opposition to a controversial coastal development. According to Reuters, earlier demonstrations targeted a luxury resort project backed by Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. The proposed development near protected coastal wetlands, which are home to flamingos, drew criticism over environmental protection and the influence of powerful investors. The protests became associated with the ‘Pink Flamingo Revolution’, with the pink flamingo serving as a symbol of opposition to the proposed luxury resort project. The movement subsequently expanded beyond environmental concerns, with protesters raising broader questions about corruption, political accountability and the government’s handling of public affairs. Three major issues are driving the demonstrations: Education concerns: Students are demanding better university facilities and standards, alongside action on the difficulties young people face in accessing quality educationCorruption allegations: Repeated corruption scandals and concerns over organised crime, including money laundering linked to drug and weapons trafficking, have fuelled criticism of governance in AlbaniaJobs and economic pressures: Young people are increasingly frustrated by limited employment opportunities and the difficulty of building a secure future, adding to dissatisfaction with the political establishment Edi Rama’s response to the protests Rama has refused to step down and blamed unspecified foreign interests for fuelling the unrest. He has also said his government is working to tackle corruption and offered to discuss students’ concerns about education costs. According to Reuters, 388 people had been charged with criminal offences during the demonstrations as of October 18. The Albanian Health Ministry said 272 people, including 169 police officers, had been injured in clashes since October 13. The European Commission has condemned the violence while reaffirming the right of people to protest peacefully. Meanwhile, the opposition Democratic Party has backed calls for political change and demanded a caretaker government and early elections, according to the Associated Press. The unrest comes as Albania seeks to join the European Union by 2030. The country is among the Western Balkan nations pursuing membership, which requires progress on democratic institutions, the rule of law and tackling corruption. Rama has argued that the escalating violence threatens this ambition rather than his government.

item.title: China's growth accelerates to 4.5% in third quarter, beats expectations
item.description: Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China's economic growth rebounded to 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, beating expectations and easing the pressure on policymakers for delivering more aggressive stimulus measures to meet the annual target. The third-quarter gross domestic product growth rate, released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Monday, beat the forecast for 4.4% growth in a Reuters poll, and improved from the more-than-three-year low of 4.3% in the April-to-June period. Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate. China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment. For January-September, the economy grew 4.6%, within the range of the government's annual growth target of 4.5%-5.0%. On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2% in the third quarter, surpassing expectation for a 1.1% rise and accelerating from 0.9% in April-June. China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus of $1.2 trillion and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners. A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade. Beijing has recently expanded support for home buyers, unveiled measures to steer cheaper credit into sectors including infrastructure and technology and allocated 550 billion yuan ($82.28 billion) in unused government debt quotas to ease local governments' financial strain and expand infrastructure investment. Authorities also stepped up fiscal support, including expanding loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers and tapping an 800 billion yuan policy-based financing tool to spur infrastructure investment. Still, infrastructure investment shrank 4.2%. Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2% in the first nine months, dropping at the same pace as in January-to-August period. Retail sales grew 1.1% in September, improving from the 0.4% rise in August and compared with an expected 0.6% rise. It marked the quickest growth since March. Property investment fell 20.6% in the first nine months in September. Policymakers refrained from releasing large-scale stimulus, as strong goods exports, aided by a global AI-fuelled tech boom, should help the country to reach its annual growth target. Industrial output expanded 5.5% in September, accelerating from the 5.2% growth in August and was in line with expectations. It marked the quickest growth in six months.
